moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Intestacy: the statutory order and the surviving spouse
subtitle: The statutory trusts and how much a surviving spouse or civil partner actually takes
objectives: State the statutory order of entitlement on intestacy created by the Administration of Estates Act 1925, as amended
Calculate a surviving spouse's entitlement — personal chattels, the statutory legacy, and any share of residue — depending on whether the deceased left issue
Apply the statutory trusts to identify who inherits, and in what shares, on a range of family structures

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the statutory order of entitlement on intestacy
Defines the statutory trusts under which issue inherit their share
Defines 'personal chattels' for the purposes of a surviving spouse's entitlement
Amended the 1925 Act: a surviving spouse with issue now takes half of residue absolutely rather than a life interest, and takes the whole estate where there is no surviving issue

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite 'the spouse gets everything' as a rough intuition, which is sometimes right and sometimes badly wrong depending on who else survived. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the statutory legacy figure — this lesson is about which family structures actually trigger it.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall of the statutory legacy and chattels definition before. The test pool below leans towards calculation-style fact patterns: expect to work out who takes what, not just recite the figures.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and make sure you can state the s 46 order and the current statutory legacy figure exactly — the later parts on calculating shares assume you already have those fixed.

overview.hook: A married man dies without a will, leaving a widow, two adult children, and an estate worth £900,000. Ask most people what happens and they'll say 'the wife gets it all.' She doesn't. The statutory formula splits the estate in a specific, calculable way that surprises almost every client hearing it for the first time — and getting that calculation right is one of the most reliably tested skills in this part of the course.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The statutory legacy figure is fixed by statutory instrument and has been increased periodically (most recently to £322,000 with effect from 26 July 2023); it is reviewed from time to time and a further increase could occur, so always confirm the current figure in practice rather than relying on memory alone.

parts.heading: The statutory order, from the top
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: When a person dies without a valid will (wholly intestate), or with a will that fails to dispose of the whole estate (partial intestacy), the Administration of Estates Act 1925, as substantially amended by the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014, dictates exactly who inherits and how much. There is no discretion and no reference to what the deceased might have wanted — only the statutory formula.

Section 46 sets the order of priority. A surviving spouse or civil partner is always dealt with first, and specially — the rules for a spouse are distinct from, and generally more generous than, the rules for any other relative. Below the spouse, the order runs: issue (children and remoter descendants) on the statutory trusts; then, only if there is no surviving spouse and no issue, parents; then siblings of the whole blood; then siblings of the half blood; then grandparents; then uncles and aunts of the whole blood, and so on down a defined list, each category only inheriting if every category above it is empty.

One relationship is conspicuously absent from this list: an unmarried cohabiting partner, however long the relationship or however much they depended on the deceased financially, has no automatic entitlement on intestacy at all. That gap is central to why so many cohabiting clients are advised to make a will.

components.definition: The mechanism under s 47 of the 1925 Act by which issue (and, further down the list, other classes of relative) inherit on intestacy: the relevant class is ascertained, and members of it take in equal shares, contingent on reaching 18 or marrying/entering a civil partnership earlier, with a substitution mechanism for a class member who predeceases leaving their own issue.

interaction.prompt: State the order of priority on intestacy, from the top, before any other relative besides a spouse or civil partner can inherit.
acceptableAnswers: spouse/civil partner first, then issue, then parents, then siblings of the whole blood
surviving spouse or civil partner, then issue on the statutory trusts, then parents, then whole-blood siblings
interaction.modelAnswer: A surviving spouse or civil partner is dealt with first and specially. Below that: issue (children and remoter descendants) on the statutory trusts; then, only if there is no surviving spouse and no issue, parents; then siblings of the whole blood; then siblings of the half blood; then grandparents; then uncles and aunts of the whole blood, and so on.

parts.heading: What the spouse takes first: chattels and the statutory legacy
parts.voice: direct — builds the calculation step by step
body: Before anyone else's share is even considered, a surviving spouse or civil partner is entitled to the deceased's personal chattels absolutely. Section 55(1)(x) defines these broadly: tangible moveable property, other than money or securities for money, property used at death solely or mainly for business purposes, or property held solely as an investment. In practice this covers most household and personal items — furniture, cars, jewellery, art collected for enjoyment rather than investment — but excludes business assets and investment holdings.

Next, the spouse takes a fixed sum, free of tax and costs, called the statutory legacy — currently £322,000. This is paid in full, with interest from the date of death, before anyone further down the order sees anything at all. If the estate (after chattels) is worth less than the statutory legacy, the spouse simply takes the whole of the remaining estate and no one else inherits under the intestacy rules.

The statutory legacy only applies where the deceased is also survived by issue. If there is no surviving issue, this two-step calculation is unnecessary — the spouse's entitlement is dealt with separately, and more generously, in Part 3.

components.citation: Administration of Estates Act 1925, s 46(1)(A) (as substituted)
components.text: If the intestate leaves a spouse or civil partner and issue, the surviving spouse or civil partner shall take the personal chattels absolutely and a fixed net sum, free of death duty and costs, together with interest ... and one half of the residue of the estate absolutely.
elements: A fixed statutory legacy (currently £322,000), free of tax and costs, with interest
One half of whatever residue remains, absolutely — only where issue also survive

interaction.prompt: A deceased is survived by a spouse and two children. The net estate, excluding chattels, is worth £250,000 — less than the statutory legacy. What happens?
options: The spouse takes the whole £250,000 plus the chattels, and the children receive nothing under the intestacy rules
The spouse takes half of £250,000 and the children split the rest equally
The children take the statutory legacy first, and the spouse only takes what is left
The estate is divided equally between the spouse and each child, per capita
interaction.explanation: The statutory legacy is a fixed sum the spouse is entitled to before residue is even calculated. Where the estate (after chattels) does not reach that figure, there is nothing left over to constitute a 'residue' at all, so the spouse takes everything and the children's entitlement to half of residue simply has nothing to bite on.

parts.heading: Splitting what's left: the half-share rule
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a worked calculation
body: Where the estate does exceed the statutory legacy, the calculation continues. After chattels and the statutory legacy are paid to the spouse, whatever remains is the residue. Under the 2014 reform, the spouse takes one half of that residue absolutely — outright, with no strings attached — and the other half is held on the statutory trusts for the deceased's issue.

This is a meaningful change from the pre-2014 law, worth knowing exists even though it is now the settled position: before 2014, a spouse in this situation only received a life interest in half of residue, with the capital ultimately passing to the issue on the spouse's own death. The 2014 Act replaced that life interest with an absolute half-share, giving the surviving spouse full ownership and control of their portion immediately.

Worked example: deceased leaves a spouse and one child; net estate (after chattels) is £722,000. The spouse takes the statutory legacy of £322,000 first. That leaves £400,000 as residue. The spouse takes half of that (£200,000) absolutely; the other half (£200,000) passes to the child on the statutory trusts. Total to the spouse: £322,000 + £200,000 = £522,000, plus the chattels.

components.title: Calculating a spouse's share where issue survive
components.description: The sequential steps for working out a surviving spouse's entitlement on intestacy where the deceased is also survived by issue.

nodes.label: Step 1: spouse takes personal chattels absolutely
Step 2: spouse takes the statutory legacy (currently £322,000) free of tax, with interest
Step 3: remaining estate is the residue
Step 4: spouse takes half of residue absolutely; the other half is held on the statutory trusts for the issue

components.textAlternative: Where a spouse and issue both survive, the calculation runs in a fixed sequence: chattels to the spouse absolutely; then the statutory legacy of £322,000 to the spouse, free of tax and with interest; then whatever remains is residue, of which the spouse takes half absolutely and the issue take the other half on the statutory trusts.

interaction.prompt: Put the steps of calculating a spouse's entitlement (where issue survive) in the correct order.
items: Spouse takes the statutory legacy of £322,000, free of tax, with interest
Whatever remains is treated as residue
Spouse takes half of residue absolutely; issue take the other half on the statutory trusts
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the fixed sequence examiners expect: chattels, then the legacy, then only whatever is left counts as residue for the 50/50 split with issue.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — the statutory legacy must be paid in full before anything is even labelled 'residue'; only the amount left after that is split with the issue.

parts.heading: No issue: the spouse takes everything
parts.voice: argumentative — states the post-2014 rule plainly, then flags what it displaced
body: Where the deceased leaves a surviving spouse but no issue, the calculation above does not apply at all — there is no statutory legacy calculation, no half-share split, and no statutory trusts to fund. The spouse simply takes the whole estate absolutely, regardless of who else survives.

This is another point the 2014 reform changed significantly. Before 2014, if the deceased left no issue but was survived by parents, or by siblings of the whole blood, those relatives shared in the estate alongside the spouse. The 2014 Act removed that sharing entirely: parents and siblings now only inherit anything on intestacy if there is no surviving spouse at all.

This produces a result some clients find counterintuitive: a childless, married deceased with close, elderly parents and no will leaves nothing to those parents — the spouse takes the entire estate. It is precisely the kind of scenario where advising a client to make a will, rather than relying on intestacy, actually changes the outcome.

components.label: No-issue scenario: what the spouse takes
points: The whole estate, absolutely — chattels, and everything else, with no statutory legacy calculation needed
Parents, siblings and other relatives take nothing while a spouse survives, even though they would inherit if there were no spouse at all
This is a post-2014 position: before the reform, some sharing with parents/siblings was possible even where a spouse survived

interaction.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by his wife and his elderly mother, but no children or other issue. Who inherits the estate?
options: The wife takes everything; the mother takes nothing under the intestacy rules
The estate is split between the wife and the mother, since both survive
The mother takes the statutory legacy and the wife takes the rest
The wife and mother share the estate equally after chattels are deducted
interaction.trapExplanation: It is tempting to assume a surviving parent must share, by analogy with how issue share residue — but the current law removed that sharing for the no-issue case entirely; a surviving spouse displaces parents (and siblings) completely.
interaction.explanation: Post-2014, where a spouse survives but there is no issue, the spouse takes the whole estate absolutely. Parents and other relatives lower in the s 46 order only inherit where there is no surviving spouse.

parts.heading: Putting it together across family structures
body: The examiner's favourite move in this topic is to vary a single fact — is there issue, or not? is the partner married, or cohabiting? — and see whether you correctly switch calculation methods. Getting the right formula depends entirely on correctly classifying the family structure first.

Four structures are worth being able to spot instantly: (1) spouse and issue survive — apply the full calculation (chattels, statutory legacy, half of residue split); (2) spouse survives, no issue — spouse takes everything, full stop; (3) no spouse, issue survive — issue take the whole estate on the statutory trusts, with no chattels or statutory legacy calculation (those only exist for a spouse); (4) no spouse and no issue — the estate cascades down the s 46 list to parents, then whole-blood siblings, and so on.

A cohabiting partner, however long the relationship, does not appear anywhere in this analysis unless they can bring a separate claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 — a different statute entirely, addressed elsewhere in this module, and not a form of automatic intestate entitlement.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students frequently apply the statutory legacy and half-residue calculation even where there is no surviving spouse at all, or apply it to a cohabiting partner as if they were legally married.
components.whyItsWrong: The statutory legacy and half-share mechanism exists only for a legally married spouse or registered civil partner. Where issue survive with no spouse, they simply take the whole estate on the statutory trusts — there is no legacy figure to deduct first. A cohabitant, however long-standing the relationship, has no entitlement under these rules at all.

interaction.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by his long-term cohabiting partner of eighteen years (never married) and two adult children from an earlier marriage. Who is entitled to the estate under the intestacy rules?
options: The cohabiting partner takes the same share a spouse would take, given the length of the relationship
The two children take the whole estate on the statutory trusts; the cohabiting partner has no automatic entitlement under these rules
The estate is split equally three ways between the partner and the two children
The children take the statutory legacy and the partner takes the residue
interaction.explanation: A cohabitant is not a 'spouse or civil partner' for these purposes, however long the relationship lasted, and has no automatic share on intestacy. With no surviving spouse, the two children simply take the whole estate on the statutory trusts in equal shares.

testPool.prompt: Which statute, as amended, governs who inherits when a person dies without a valid will disposing of their whole estate?
options: The Administration of Estates Act 1925, as amended by the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014
The Wills Act 1837
The Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975
The Trustee Act 2000
testPool.explanation: The 1925 Act, substantially amended by the 2014 Act, sets the statutory order of entitlement and the statutory trusts governing intestate succession.

testPool.prompt: Under s 55(1)(x) of the Administration of Estates Act 1925, which of the following is correctly classified as a 'personal chattel' passing to a surviving spouse absolutely?
options: Shares held by the deceased purely as an investment
A car used personally by the deceased, not for business purposes
Cash held in a bank account
Equipment used solely for the deceased's sole-trader business
testPool.explanation: Personal chattels covers tangible moveable property used personally, such as a car, but expressly excludes money, investment property, and assets used solely or mainly for business purposes.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by a spouse and one adult child. The net estate, excluding chattels, is worth £900,000. How much does the spouse receive in total, before chattels?
options: £450,000 (half of the whole estate)
£611,000 — the statutory legacy plus half of the remaining residue
£900,000 — the spouse takes everything regardless of the child
testPool.explanation: The spouse takes the statutory legacy of £322,000 first. That leaves £578,000 as residue, of which the spouse takes half (£289,000). Total: £322,000 + £289,000 = £611,000, plus chattels separately.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by a spouse and three children. The net estate, excluding chattels, is worth £322,000 exactly. What happens?
options: The spouse takes the whole £322,000 and the children receive nothing under the intestacy rules, because there is no residue left to split
Each child receives an equal share of £322,000 alongside the spouse
The spouse takes half and the children split the other half three ways
The statutory legacy does not apply where there is more than one child, so the children take priority
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes assume the number of children changes how the statutory legacy is calculated. It does not — the legacy is a fixed sum to the spouse regardless of how many children survive; only what remains after it is split with the issue, and here nothing remains.
testPool.explanation: The statutory legacy is paid to the spouse in full before residue is calculated. Where the estate exactly equals (or falls short of) the legacy figure, there is no residue left, so the spouse takes the whole estate and the children receive nothing under the intestacy rules — irrespective of how many children there are.

testPool.prompt: What is the current statutory legacy a surviving spouse is entitled to (in addition to personal chattels) where the deceased also leaves issue?
testPool.explanation: The statutory legacy currently stands at £322,000, effective from 26 July 2023, and is reviewed from time to time by statutory instrument.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by a spouse but no children, grandchildren, or other issue of any kind. The net estate is worth £1.2 million. How is it distributed?
options: The spouse takes the statutory legacy and half of residue; the rest passes to the deceased's parents
The spouse takes the whole estate absolutely; no other relative inherits under the intestacy rules
The estate is split equally between the spouse and any surviving siblings
The spouse takes only the chattels, and the rest passes down the statutory order
testPool.explanation: Where a spouse survives and there is no issue, the statutory legacy and half-residue calculation does not apply at all. The spouse takes the entire estate absolutely, and no other relative inherits anything under the intestacy rules.

testPool.prompt: How did the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014 change a surviving spouse's entitlement to half of residue where issue also survive?
options: It removed the spouse's entitlement to any share of residue at all
It replaced a life interest in half of residue with an absolute (outright) half-share
It increased the spouse's share of residue from a half to two-thirds
It made no change to the residue calculation, only to the statutory legacy figure
testPool.explanation: Before the 2014 reform, a spouse in this position took only a life interest in half of residue, with the capital ultimately passing to the issue. The 2014 Act converted this into an absolute half-share, giving the spouse full and immediate ownership.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by two children but no spouse or civil partner. The net estate is worth £600,000. How is it distributed?
options: The estate is held on the statutory trusts for the two children, who take equal shares once they meet the conditions (e.g. reaching 18)
£322,000 passes to the children and the remainder passes to the deceased's parents
The children each receive a life interest only, with capital passing to grandchildren
The estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia because there is no spouse
testPool.explanation: With no surviving spouse, the statutory legacy and half-residue mechanism (which exists only for a spouse) is irrelevant. The whole estate is simply held on the statutory trusts for the issue, who take equal shares.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following correctly states the current position on cohabiting (unmarried) partners under the intestacy rules?
options: A cohabitant of five years or more is treated the same as a spouse
A cohabitant has no automatic entitlement on intestacy, regardless of the length of the relationship, though a separate claim may be possible under different legislation
A cohabitant automatically receives the statutory legacy but not a share of residue
A cohabitant is treated as 'issue' if they have children with the deceased
testPool.trapExplanation: A common error is assuming a period of cohabitation (sometimes confused with 'common law marriage', which does not exist in English law) creates automatic intestacy rights. It does not — only a separate claim under the Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 may be available, and that is a discretionary claim, not automatic entitlement.
testPool.explanation: However long a couple has cohabited, an unmarried partner has no automatic entitlement under the intestacy rules. Their only recourse is a discretionary claim under separate legislation, which is a fundamentally different mechanism from automatic statutory entitlement.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate, survived by his wife and his adult daughter from a previous relationship. The estate (excluding chattels) is worth £522,000. What is the daughter's share of residue?
options: £100,000 — half of the £200,000 residue remaining after the statutory legacy
£261,000 — half of the whole estate
£522,000 — the whole estate, since the wife is not the daughter's biological mother
Nothing — stepchildren and children from previous relationships have no entitlement
testPool.explanation: The spouse takes the £322,000 statutory legacy first, leaving £200,000 as residue. That residue is split equally between spouse and issue: the daughter, as the sole surviving child, takes the whole issue-share of residue, £100,000. (A child's biological relationship to the deceased governs their status as issue — the wife's relationship to the child is irrelevant to the child's own entitlement.)

testPool.prompt: Under the current (post-2014) statutory order, when do a deceased's parents inherit anything on intestacy?
options: Whenever the deceased leaves no children, regardless of whether a spouse survives
Only where there is no surviving spouse and no surviving issue
Only where the deceased's estate exceeds £322,000
Parents can never inherit under the intestacy rules
testPool.explanation: Post-2014, parents only inherit where both the spouse and issue categories are empty — no surviving spouse and no surviving issue at all. A surviving spouse displaces parents entirely, even where there is no issue.

testPool.prompt: Which best describes the function of the 'statutory trusts' under s 47 of the Administration of Estates Act 1925?
options: They define the mechanism by which issue (and other classes lower in the s 46 order) inherit their share, including provision for a class member who predeceases leaving their own issue
They are a tax-avoidance structure used only for estates over the statutory legacy figure
They apply only where the deceased left a valid will
They determine which relatives are entitled to act as personal representatives
testPool.explanation: The statutory trusts under s 47 govern how a defined class of relatives (issue, or further down the list) share the relevant portion of the estate, including a substitution mechanism analogous to anti-lapse where a class member predeceases leaving their own issue.

testPool.prompt: A deceased dies intestate with no surviving spouse, no issue, and no surviving parents, but is survived by one full sibling and one half-sibling (sharing only one parent with the deceased). Who inherits, and how?
options: The full sibling and half-sibling share the estate equally, since both are siblings
The full sibling takes the whole estate; siblings of the half blood only inherit if there is no surviving sibling of the whole blood
The half-sibling takes priority because they are younger
Neither sibling inherits; the estate passes to the Crown
testPool.explanation: The s 46 order places siblings of the whole blood ahead of siblings of the half blood. Where a whole-blood sibling survives, they take the estate (on the statutory trusts, if more than one) and the half-blood sibling's category is not reached at all.

testPool.prompt: A deceased is survived by a spouse and one child. The net estate (excluding chattels) is worth exactly £322,000. Which statement correctly describes the outcome?
options: The spouse takes the full £322,000 and the child takes nothing, because there is no surplus to constitute residue
The spouse and child split £322,000 equally because both categories survive
The child takes the statutory legacy since children have priority over spouses for the first tranche
The estate passes entirely to the child because the statutory legacy only applies where there is no issue
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to assume that because 'issue survive', they must automatically get something. But the calculation is sequential: the statutory legacy is paid to the spouse in full first, and only genuine surplus above that figure becomes residue for the issue to share in.
testPool.explanation: The statutory legacy is satisfied in full before any residue is identified. An estate exactly equal to the statutory legacy leaves nothing over, so the spouse takes the whole £322,000 and the child receives nothing under the intestacy rules on these facts.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is applying the spouse's statutory legacy and half-residue calculation to the wrong family structure — either where there is no surviving spouse at all (issue simply take everything) or where there is no surviving issue (the spouse simply takes everything). Classify the family structure correctly before reaching for any figure.
